overview:
Two angels reach Sodom at evening, and Lot, sitting in the gate, presses them to stay at his house. The men of the city, young and old, surround the house and demand the guests. Lot goes out, offers his daughters instead, and is pulled back inside as the attackers are struck blind. At dawn the angels take Lot, his wife and daughters by the hand and lead them out. Lot bargains to flee to little Zoar; fire and brimstone fall, and his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Later, in a cave, his daughters make him drunk and conceive Moab and Ammon.

Notice whose rescue this is. Lot lingers and has to be led out by the hand, yet the narrator credits his escape to Abraham, who had stood before the LORD pleading for the city: “God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out” (v. 29).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith's revision of Genesis (June 1830–March 1831) changes vv. 1, 8–10, 12, 31 and 35 (JST Genesis 19:1, 9–15, 18, 37, 39).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The evening and morning after chapter 18 (vv. 1, 27), in Abraham's ninety-ninth year. Traditional dating places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Sodom and the cities of the Jordan plain (13:10–12), traditionally sought near the south end of the Dead Sea; then Zoar, and a cave in the hills.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Judges 19:22–25 (a near-identical mob scene at Gibeah); Jubilees 16:5–9; Josephus, Antiquities 1.11.3–5.

hermeneutics:
City gates were where business was done and disputes were judged. In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat, Danel sits at the gate to decide the cases of widows and orphans, and Israel's elders do the same (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–2). Lot “sat in the gate” (v. 1), a sign that he has become a man of standing in Sodom. The mob's sneer in v. 9, that this newcomer “will needs be a judge,” shows they still count him an outsider.

The Dead Sea basin is a country of salt, bitumen and sulfur. Genesis already mentions its bitumen pits (14:10). Strabo describes asphalt rising from the lake, scorched rocks and ashy soil on its shore, and Tacitus speaks of a burnt plain that once held great cities. At the southwest end the salt ridge of Jebel Usdum, “Mount Sodom,” weathers into upright columns. First hearers knew a dead, smoking landscape, and a story like v. 26 explains a landmark they could picture.

Moab and Ammon were real kingdoms east of the Jordan in Israel's time; the Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) speaks for a king of Moab and his god Chemosh. Peoples told origin stories about their neighbors, and this one does two things at once. It makes Moab and Ammon Israel's kin through Abraham's nephew, and it gives them a shameful birth. Deuteronomy uses both: Israel may not take their land, given to “the children of Lot” (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19), yet they are barred from the assembly (23:3).

notes: **Where the panels break:** Abraham's guests leave him with a promise; Lot's guests are besieged, and the guests end up rescuing their host (v. 10).
**Key words:** “overthrow” comes three times (vv. 21, 25, 29), and “the cry” of the city (v. 13) picks up 18:20–21.
**Looking:** Lot is told not to look behind him (v. 17); his wife looks back (v. 26); next morning Abraham looks toward Sodom from the place where he had stood before the LORD (vv. 27–28).

The Sodom story runs from 18:16 to 19:29, and the cave scene (vv. 30–38) closes Lot's part in Genesis; he is not mentioned again. The wording of v. 29 echoes the Flood's “God remembered Noah” (8:1), and Abraham's view of the smoke (v. 28) closes the scene that opened with him looking toward Sodom (18:16).
**Links:** Sodom becomes the Bible's byword for judgment (Isaiah 1:9–10; Matthew 10:15). Moab returns through Ruth, great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:13–17).

traditions.text: In the JST the mob is angry with Lot and demands his daughters as well as the guests. Lot does not offer the girls; he pleads with the crowd not to take them, saying “God will not justify his servant in this thing,” and asks them to let the strangers have peace in his house. The angels of God who pull him inside are described as holy men.

Other JST readings run through the chapter. Three angels, not two, come to Sodom, matching the three at Mamre, and Lot's guests are “these holy men.” At the end the JST passes judgment where Genesis is silent: the firstborn “dealt wickedly,” and both daughters “did wickedly.”

The prophet names Sodom's sins as Jerusalem's sister: “pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness,” and failing to strengthen the hand of the poor and needy. Then she grew haughty and “committed abomination.” Later Jewish writers built on this verse, and Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer quotes it directly.

Lists Lot among the righteous whom Wisdom saved, the man who fled the fire that fell on “the five cities.” The smoking waste land, plants whose fruit never ripens, and “a standing pillar of salt” remain as witnesses. The pillar, it says, is a monument of an unbelieving soul.

Says the cities were burned for their uncleanness and fornication, and warns that God will judge any place that acts like Sodom. It calls the sin of Lot and his daughters one that had not been on the earth since Adam, and says the heavenly tablets decree a like judgment on his descendants.

Sodom grew proud from its wealth, unjust to men and impious to God, and “hated strangers.” Lot's wife kept turning back, too curious about the city's fate, and became a pillar of salt. Josephus adds his own testimony: “For I have seen it, and it remains at this day.”

Why salt? Genesis Rabbah says Lot's wife sinned through salt: she went to the neighbors asking for salt for her guests, so the town would learn they were there. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan says she was a daughter of Sodom who looked back to see what would become of her father's house, and was punished by the salt she sinned with.
traditions.cite: Genesis Rabbah 51:5; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 19:26

traditions.text: Describes Sodom as a city that grew rich and made cruelty to travelers its law. Guests were laid on a bed and stretched or cut to fit it; beggars were given marked coins that no one would take for bread. A young woman who smuggled bread to the poor was smeared with honey and left on the wall for the bees, and that, Rav says, is the “great” cry of 18:20.

Jesus compares his coming to Lot's day, when people ate, bought, planted and built until fire fell, and adds, “Remember Lot's wife.” Second Peter calls Lot a just man vexed day after day by what he saw and heard in Sodom, making him a model of God's rescue of the godly.

Clement of Rome says Lot was saved because of his hospitality and godliness. His wife, of a different mind, became a pillar of salt “unto this day,” a sign that the double-minded who doubt God's power bring judgment on themselves. Josephus, writing about the same years, also says the pillar could still be seen.

Passes on a teaching from an older presbyter: where Scripture records a patriarch's deed without blaming it, readers should not condemn it. Lot's daughters, thinking all mankind had perished, acted to preserve the race and are to be excused. The pillar of salt that still stands becomes a figure of the Church, the salt of the earth.

Treats the fire on Sodom as a preview of the last judgment. The command not to look back, he says, means that those reborn by grace must not turn back in heart to the life they left. Lot's wife, turned to salt, became a seasoning for believers, a warning to savor.

A Greek geographer describing the Dead Sea region. Near Masada he notes scorched rocks, ashy soil and dripping pitch, and repeats the local report that thirteen cities once stood there with Sodom as their capital. Earthquakes, eruptions of fire, and hot waters full of asphalt and sulfur destroyed them, some swallowed and some abandoned.

The Roman historian reports a plain near the lake that was once fertile and held great cities, later burned by lightning, where the ground still looks scorched and plants wither. He grants that cities may have been destroyed by fire from heaven, but blames the lake's fumes for the barren soil.
